frozen_original.synopsis: The New York Attorney General's investigation, culminating in a November 2019 court order, found that the Donald J. Trump Foundation functioned as a personal checkbook for Trump's business expenses, legal settlements, and political activities. Specific violations included a $100,000 Foundation payment to settle legal claims against Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort, a $158,000 payment to settle a claim against his Trump National Golf Club, and a $10,000 purchase at a charity auction of a portrait of Trump himself — later displayed at Trump National Doral. In the lead-up to the 2016 Iowa caucuses, Trump's campaign used $2.8 million in Foundation funds raised from the public at a televised fundraiser to boost his political standing. A New York Supreme Court judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages; Trump admitted personally misusing Foundation funds in 19 factual admissions. The Foundation was dissolved under court supervision in December 2018, and Trump accepted a five-year ban on heading any New York charity.
frozen_original.title: Charity as Piggy Bank: Trump Foundation Dissolved for Persistent Illegal Self-Dealing

proposal.description_long: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held a nationally televised fundraiser in Iowa for veterans’ organizations while skipping a televised Republican debate. The New York Attorney General’s court filings say the event raised approximately $5.6 million and that $2.823 million of that amount was donated to the Trump Foundation, which was then expected to distribute the money to veterans’ groups. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation ceded control of the grants to Trump’s campaign, making the Foundation’s contribution an improper in-kind campaign contribution. That allegation and the eventual resolution belong to the later legal case; they should not be described as a finding that every fundraiser dollar was misused. In November 2019, a court separately ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages to charities and imposed restrictions related to future charitable service. The stored January 28, 2016 date identifies the fundraiser, not that later court order. This draft aligns the title and descriptions with the dated fundraiser and clearly distinguishes the event from the judgment. The record should not combine the two dates or imply that the court order occurred in 2016.

This fundraiser is separate from the $2 million damages order issued in 2019.
